children: America is attempting the largest infrastructure buildout in its modern history. The bill, by one academic estimate, comes to $10.3 trillion.
The headline figure comes from a 2026 paper by Stijn van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School. He projects $10.3 trillion in US AI infrastructure investment between 2025 and 2032.

Spread across those years, that works out to about 3.63% of US GDP annually. For historical comparison, the paper points to the railroad buildout of the late 19th century. That era peaked at roughly 2.2% of GDP.
A large share of the spending sits with the hyperscalers: Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet, and Oracle. Their capital expenditures are projected at $4.2 trillion through 2029.

That spending is expected to surpass their operating cash flow by 2026. Even the richest companies on Earth would need to lean primarily on external capital to fund the buildout, according to the research.
Constraints in power supply, shortages of skilled workers, and construction delays are all slowing projects.
Google has cited expected grid connection delays of five to ten years, driven by data center demand. The pressure is particularly acute in regional grids such as PJM and ERCOT.
The research also flags a potential power shortfall of up to 68 GW for data centers.
The AI industry would need roughly $3.7 trillion in annual revenue by 2032 to support the projected investment. Current revenue estimates from major players sit around $100 billion.
The International Monetary Fund has taken notice. As of October 2026, the IMF warned of potential stock price corrections if profitability on AI investment trends downward.

For investors, the clearest pressure point is the reliance on external financing. When hyperscaler capex outruns operating cash flow, the buildout becomes sensitive to credit conditions and investor appetite.

The concentration of spending among five companies also matters. Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet, and Oracle carry heavy weight in major equity indexes, so their capex decisions ripple well beyond tech portfolios.

The research notes a broader systemic concern as well. Capital flowing toward AI could pull funding away from traditional sectors, raising questions about financial stability if the bet underdelivers.
Grid delays in regions like PJM and ERCOT could decide which projects get built on schedule and which wait years for electricity.
The key metric through 2032 is revenue growth. Watch whether AI income starts climbing meaningfully from the roughly $100 billion level toward the $3.7 trillion the buildout implies.

title: America’s $10 trillion AI infrastructure boom is starting to show strain
